answer.evidence: The stairs descend as a stack of brown tread bands, each 4-7 rows tall. Each band ends in a 1-row light nosing line (rows 12, 18, 26, 35, 44) followed by 2 rows of dark shadow (rows 13-14, 19-20, 27-28, 36-37, 45-47), the usual top-surface pattern. The treads step wider toward the bottom, which adds depth. Brown side posts and walls frame the stairs as vertical faces, and the dark riser shadows plus the side posts give a front face of 3+ rows. The lintel at rows 0-2 is a front-facing beam with a light line at row 1, but the stairs, not the lintel, are the main body.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a wooden staircase-down tile in a frame. It reads as a prop rather than a wall face, but it is judged against wall references of the same kind. The measured facts show 9 visible tones per tile against 17 and 13 for the references, so it is lower but not extremely so. Near-flat coverage is 8% against 0% for both references, so there are some flat areas, though not large ones. 69% of the dark edge pixels are near-neutral against 12-13% for the references, so the outline leans toward a neutral dark line. By eye, the frame outline looks dark brown-black and only weakly tinted. Wood steps show about 3-4 tones, with some plank highlights but little grain. The references have 5-6 steps with per-stone and per-timber texture, plaster speckle and tinted dark edges. The candidate is cleanly drawn but flatter and more sticker-like than the references, with fewer tones and a neutral-leaning outline.

answer.evidence: The main body is a flight of steps. Each step is a brown tread band of 4-5 rows (e.g. rows 30-34 at x=16) that ends in a light front-edge line (row 35, L=169) followed by 2 rows of dark shadow (rows 36-37), and this repeats at rows 22-28 and 39-47. That is evidence (a) for a top surface. The dark riser/shadow rows give a front face of about 3 rows per step. The side walls and pillars and the 3-row lintel at rows 0-2 are drawn only as front-facing vertical strips with no top slope, so not every major part shows a top. The stair treads still carry the main volume and read as three-quarter.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a wooden stairs-down piece in a frame. It has about 4 wood steps (light tan, mid brown, dark brown, deep) and a few texture dots on the treads. Visible tones per tile are 9 against 17 and 13 for the references, so it is clearly lower, though not flat (8% near-flat against 0%). 69% of its dark edge pixels are near-neutral, against 12-13% for the references. That points to a dark, near-black outline around the frame, closer to the sticker look than the references' material-tinted edges, though some brown lean is visible. The treads and risers are fairly smooth, with little grain or per-plank highlighting, while the references carry speckle plaster and individually shaded stones. A careful artist would find this thinner and flatter than the references, so it fails on shallow shading and the near-neutral outline.

answer.evidence: The main body is a descending staircase. Each step is a brown tread band of 5-6 rows (e.g. 21-25 and 29-34), ending in a 1-row light front-edge line (rows 18, 26, 35, 44) followed by 2 rows of dark shadow or riser (19-20, 27-28, 36-37). That matches evidence (a), a top band with an edge line and shadow, repeated on every step. The top rows 0-2 are a front-facing lintel strip, which does not count as a top surface. The side walls are vertical faces flanking the stair, and the stair itself shows a top surface on each step, so the reading is three-quarter.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small wooden stairs-down prop (a dark frame around a few light plank steps), not a wall face, so it does not match the reference kind well. Read as a wall-like piece, it is shallow. Its steps show about 3 lightness tones on the wood: a light plank, a mid tone and a dark frame. Its visible tones per tile are 9 against 17 and 13 in the references. The dark edge pixels are 69% near-neutral, against 12-13% in the references, so the outline reads as a neutral dark line around the shapes, the sticker look, not a tinted dark material tone. The steps are mostly smooth bands with little grain, speckle or per-plank highlights, unlike the plaster speckle and stone-by-stone shading in the references. Near-flat coverage is 8% against 0%. It looks thinner and flatter than the references, so it fails.

answer.evidence: The main body is a descending staircase. Each step has a brown tread band 4-7 rows tall (rows 15-17, 21-25, 29-34, 38-43) that ends in a light front-edge line (rows 18, 26, 35, 44) followed by 2 rows of dark shadow or riser (rows 19-20, 27-28, 36-37, 45-47). This is evidence (a) repeated at every step, and the top tread (rows 10-12) is lit. The dark risers and side frame posts form the vertical faces, so the object reads as a top surface with a front face and is not a flat slab or a pure elevation. Rows 0-2 are a front-facing beam strip with no top surface, but it is a minor part.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a wooden staircase-down prop, about one tile wide and two tiles tall. It reads as a wall-kind piece only loosely. It shows about 4 brown wood steps: highlight on the step edges, mid, dark and a deep recess. The measured facts put it at 9 visible tones per tile against 17 and 13 for the references, so it is lower but not far off. Near-flat coverage is 8% against 0% for both references, so there are a few flat areas. Of its dark edge pixels, 69% are near-neutral, against 12-13% for the references. That leans toward a black sticker-style outline, though the picture shows some brown tint on the frame, so I call it mixed. The step treads are fairly clean bands with little grain or per-plank speckle, whereas the references carry plaster speckle, per-stone shading and timber grain. Overall the shading is shallower, the outline is partly neutral and the texture is thinner than the references. A careful artist would not accept it beside them without it looking flatter.
